segments.title: Laïd Sebaï — The murder on Rue Louis-le-Grand
segments.text:
Look at this doorway.

Our story begins here, in July nineteen seventy-five.

During the night of the twenty-sixth to the twenty-seventh of July, sometime between two and half past two in the morning, much of Paris is asleep.

Then an explosion tears through the quiet outside the offices of the Amicale des Algériens en Europe, on Rue Louis-le-Grand.

A bomb has exploded outside the building.

The material damage here is relatively limited, and no casualties are reported.

But this is no isolated incident.

At almost the same moment, two more explosive devices strike premises belonging to the same organisation. One in Lyon. Another in Roubaix.

Three cities. Three buildings connected to the same organisation. And three explosions within a very short space of time.

In Lyon, the blast is powerful enough to shatter windows as far as eighty metres away. The damage in Roubaix is substantial too.

Here in Paris, the building at number twenty-three Rue Louis-le-Grand suffers less.

But the message is unmistakable. The Amicale des Algériens en Europe is being targeted in a coordinated series of bomb attacks.

In a statement, the organisation condemns another attack added to what it describes as a long sequence of violence.

Who planted the bombs?

Why attack three French cities at almost exactly the same time?

And who is trying to reach the organisation's leaders?

The first news reports do not clearly identify the perpetrators.

For now, remember one address. Number twenty-three, Rue Louis-le-Grand.

Because a little more than two years later, another tragedy will unfold in the entrance hall of this building.

This time, the damage will not be confined to bricks and glass.

The months pass. Yet attacks against Algerian interests in France do not come to an end.

In the autumn of nineteen seventy-seven, tensions rise sharply.

On the fourth of November, an explosion strikes premises connected with Algerian interests near the Avenue de l'Opéra.

A few days later, more alarming news reaches the Algerian community.

On the fifteenth of November, the newspaper Le Monde publishes a disturbing report: two Algerians are said to have been abducted in Paris.

The story concerns an operation attributed to a group invoking the name Charles Martel, against a backdrop of tension over French citizens held by the Polisario Front.

The reported abduction appears in the press, but its exact date and circumstances are not completely established.

What matters is that the violence is no longer being described simply as damage to buildings. Men are now being reported as hostages.

Then comes the twenty-ninth of November.

Another explosion targets Algerian interests in the Opéra district.

We are now just three days away from the killing of Laïd Sebaï.

Look again at this entrance.

Two years earlier, a bomb had exploded outside these premises. Now fresh attacks are taking place nearby.

Threats and acts of violence are mounting.

We cannot establish that the same group was responsible for all these incidents.

But one thing is certain: when we reach the morning of the second of December, nineteen seventy-seven, the murder does not emerge from a peaceful background.

It follows a succession of attacks and alarms.

That Friday morning, Laïd Sebaï is finishing his shift.

He does not yet know that he will never go home.

It is Friday, the second of December, nineteen seventy-seven. Around half past nine in the morning.

Inside the Amicale's premises, a night watchman is coming to the end of his duty.

His name is Laïd Sebaï.

He is forty-six years old, and the father of seven children.

He is preparing to leave for home.

But armed men are waiting inside the building.

What happens next will make this address the scene of something far more tragic.

Because Laïd Sebaï is about to be murdered.

And there is a possibility that the killers have mistaken him for somebody else.

To understand why, we need to meet the man they may actually have intended to kill.

Abdelkrim Ghraieb.

At the time, Ghraieb is president of the Amicale des Algériens en Europe.

But that title tells us only part of his story.

During the Algerian War, he held positions of responsibility within the French federation of the National Liberation Front, or FLN.

After Algerian independence in nineteen sixty-two, the Amicale occupied an important place in relations between the Algerian authorities and the Algerian community living in France.

Ghraieb had connections and influence extending well beyond the walls of this street.

According to several historical accounts, the organisation's president and its night watchman bore a degree of physical resemblance, including a similar build.

And that resemblance may have cost Sebaï his life.

Let's return to the scene of the crime, while keeping two different accounts carefully apart.

The newspaper Rouge, reporting the following day, places the shooting in the entrance hall.

Sebaï is struck by several bullets and dies inside the building.

The paper says that after he falls, two Amicale employees who have just entered the lift to reach their offices are also fired upon.

The bullets miss them.

A later historical account describes a different sequence of movements. In that version, Sebaï had come downstairs with two people who took refuge in the lift.

So the sources do not entirely agree.

We have not found a reliable identification of those two survivors.

And we have no proof that Ghraieb was one of them.

Was Laïd Sebaï the intended target?

The possibility that he was mistaken for Abdelkrim Ghraieb appears very early in press coverage.

If the theory is correct, the gunmen killed the watchman while looking for an influential official of the organisation.

But we must not turn a hypothesis into a judicial finding.

We know armed men opened fire, and that Sebaï died.

We also know that, according to the contemporary newspaper account, other employees were shot at.

What we do not know with certainty is what the gunmen had in mind.

Very soon afterwards, an anonymous caller claims responsibility for the murder in the name of Delta.

That name recalls the commando units associated with the Secret Army Organisation, the OAS, during the Algerian War.

Fifteen years after Algerian independence, the choice of name carries a powerful meaning.

But a claim of responsibility is not a verified signature.

The callers say they are acting in retaliation for the detention of French citizens by the Polisario Front in Mauritania.

They threaten further violence against Algerians living in France.

The Algerian ambassador, Mohammed Bedjaoui, condemns the threats.

Trade unions, associations and political organisations protest.

Laïd Sebaï's body is repatriated to Algeria, where he is buried in the martyrs' section of El Alia cemetery.

For his family, the questions go far beyond the anonymous claims. Seven children have lost their father.

But the story does not end there.

On the fourth of May, nineteen seventy-eight, in the fifth arrondissement, another man is murdered near the lift of his building, at number four Rue Rollin.

His name is Henri Curiel.

He was on his way to a yoga class.

Curiel was born in Egypt. A communist activist and later an internationalist, he had helped networks supporting the Algerian National Liberation Front during the Algerian War.

Afterwards, he became involved with several anti-colonial movements.

He also worked to encourage contacts between Israelis and Palestinians.

His activities brought hostility and surveillance.

According to several contemporary sources, two armed men were waiting for him.

Curiel is killed.

Once again, the name Delta appears in a claim of responsibility.

The similarities are troubling.

Two murders in Paris. Two men connected in different ways to the history of Algerian independence. Attacks near lifts. And the same name appearing in claims of responsibility.

But similarities are not proof.

For that, we have to turn to ballistics.

On the twelfth of May, nineteen seventy-eight, Le Monde reports that one of the pistols used against Sebaï, a weapon of eleven point four three millimetre calibre, was also used in Curiel's murder.

The same gun.

Five months apart.

This time, the connection is physical evidence.

Yet the ballistic match does not identify the gunman, or the person who ordered either killing.

Investigators try to understand which organisations and networks might have been involved.

Former OAS militants, possible clandestine political networks, and possible links to intelligence services all become subjects of investigation.

The investigating judge, Guy Joly, encounters difficulties obtaining certain documents and securing interviews.

Questions surrounding the case persist for decades.

In his own account of events, the former police commissioner Lucien Aimé-Blanc implicates Jean-Pierre Maïone-Libaude.

Later, René Resciniti de Says claims, in testimony made public after his death, that he took part in the murder of Curiel.

He names Pierre Debizet, a leader of the Service d'action civique, as the alleged person who ordered it.

These are not judicial convictions.

Resciniti's account, including his claim about the supposed origin of a weapon, requires independent verification.

In October twenty twenty, a former inspector with France's domestic intelligence service, Marc Ducarre, is detained for questioning in the Curiel investigation.

He is released without prosecution at the end of that period of custody.

The names emerging from the case do not, by themselves, solve the murder.

Yet the investigation remains active.

In twenty twenty-five, magistrate Emmanuelle Ducos, working at the national unit for serial or unresolved crimes in Nanterre, requests the declassification of documents relating to the Curiel case.

In February twenty twenty-six, the French official gazette publishes another favourable opinion concerning the release of a series of notes and records.

That is not a verdict.

Nor is it proof that those archives contain the answer.

It tells us that investigators are still seeking to compare once-protected information with the rest of the evidence.

Now let us return to the man whose name began this story.

Look again at this doorway.

In July nineteen seventy-five, a bomb had already exploded outside the Amicale's premises.

In November nineteen seventy-seven, Algerian interests in Paris faced renewed attacks.

And then Laïd Sebaï was murdered at the end of his night shift.

Perhaps he was mistaken for the Amicale's president, Abdelkrim Ghraieb.

Ghraieb survived. He continued his career and became Algeria's ambassador to Iran, taking part in diplomacy surrounding the release of the American hostages in January nineteen eighty-one.

The contrast is striking.

The man who may have been the target went on to an international career.

The man who died left behind seven children.

Then a single gun created a material link between Sebaï's killing and the murder of Henri Curiel.

Almost half a century later, secret documents are still the subject of judicial requests.

We do not know whether those responsible for the bombings in nineteen seventy-five, the attacks in November nineteen seventy-seven and the murders belonged to the same networks.

We know the events followed one another.

We know one weapon was used in two killings.

And we know the possibility of mistaken identity has existed since the earliest stages of the investigation.

Why did Laïd Sebaï die that morning?

We can tell you what the historical records establish.

We cannot close the case on behalf of the investigators.

Now we leave the nineteen seventies behind.

Just a few steps away, another story awaits us, among the extraordinary collections of Joséphine de Beauharnais.
